chapters.title: Chapter 8: Careers and the Business of Market Making in India

lessons.title: Breaking In: How Quant Researchers and Prop Trading Applicants Actually Get Hired

body.text: These interviews are not really testing whether you can recite a formula. They are testing whether you can reason about a market under uncertainty, out loud, in real time, which is exactly what this entire course has been building toward.

children.text: Quant research and prop trading hiring at firms in this space commonly follows a recognisable pattern: an online quantitative aptitude test covering probability, mental arithmetic, and logic puzzles, a coding round testing problem-solving in Python or a systems language depending on the role, one or more live trading game or market making simulation rounds, and finally technical and behavioural conversations with the desk itself. The exact order and emphasis varies by firm and by whether the role is research-focused or development-focused, but this general shape is common enough across the industry to be worth preparing for specifically.
Why Trading Games Test Exactly What This Course Covers

A classic live interview exercise gives a candidate an unknown underlying value, sometimes literally a hidden card or die roll, and asks them to quote a two-sided market on it, sometimes across several rounds with trades actually happening against the candidate's quotes. This is not a trick question layered on top of unrelated material; it is a compressed, live version of Chapter 1's core loop, quoting both sides, and Chapter 4's adverse selection problem, since the interviewer often plays an informed counterparty some fraction of the time. A candidate who has internalised why a wider spread is the correct response to a higher informed fraction, rather than only being able to state the Glosten-Milgrom formula from memory, visibly performs better in these rounds, because the reasoning transfers to variations the interviewer introduces on the spot.

body.title: A Live Trading Game, Revisited
body.prompt: In a mock interview, you are told the underlying value is ₹110 or ₹90, each equally likely, exactly as in Chapter 4's worked example, but this interviewer plays the informed trader 70% of the time rather than 30%, always buying at ₹110 and selling at ₹90, with the remaining 30% of the time trading randomly. Using the same Bayesian approach from Chapter 4, what ask price should you quote, in rupees?
body.explanation: With an informed fraction of 70%, P(buy | ₹110) = 0.7 + 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.85, and P(buy | ₹90) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15. Since both states are equally likely, P(buy) = 0.5. E[Value | buy] = (0.85 × 0.5 × 110 + 0.15 × 0.5 × 90) ÷ 0.5 = 53.5 ÷ 0.5 = ₹107. By the same symmetry as Chapter 4's original example, the bid would be ₹93, giving a ₹14 spread, more than double the ₹6 spread from the original 30%-informed version, exactly reflecting how much more dangerous this counterparty is.

body.text: Notice what just happened: a genuine interview-style question was answered using nothing more than material already covered in this course. That is precisely the point of building real conceptual fluency rather than memorising isolated formulas, since interviewers routinely vary the specific numbers, and only genuine understanding survives that variation.

children.text: A significant share of hiring in this space in India happens through campus recruiting at institutions known for strong quantitative talent, engineering institutes, statistics and mathematics programmes, and computer science departments among them. A background in competitive programming or mathematical olympiads is often treated as a useful signal, not because either is directly relevant to trading, but because both demonstrate exactly the fast, precise, pressure-tested quantitative reasoning these interviews are built to test. This is not the only path in: candidates without that specific background do break in through strong independent projects, demonstrated market microstructure knowledge, and a portfolio of applied analysis that speaks for itself.
What Actually Differentiates a Strong Application

Being able to explain why a formula works, not just state it, consistently distinguishes stronger candidates in these interviews. A concrete way to build and demonstrate this is through independent projects that directly replicate the analyses covered in this course: estimating an effective spread on real NSE data using the Roll model from Chapter 2, estimating PIN or VPIN on a real stock's trade data from Chapter 4, or building and backtesting a simple reservation-price-based quoting simulation using the Avellaneda-Stoikov intuition from Chapter 3. Work like this, done on real Indian market data rather than a textbook example, gives a candidate something specific and defensible to discuss, which tends to matter more in these interviews than a longer but shallower list of generic skills.

body.text: Specific hiring processes, test formats, and role requirements vary by firm and change over time. The pattern described in this lesson reflects common practice broadly observed across this industry, not a guaranteed or universal process at any specific employer; treat it as useful preparation context, not a fixed checklist.

body.title: What a Trading Game Round Is Actually Testing
body.question: What is the primary purpose of a live trading game or market making simulation round in these interviews?
options: To test whether a candidate has memorised the exact wording of academic papers
To test whether a candidate can reason about pricing under uncertainty and adverse selection in real time, adapting to variations on the spot
To test typing speed under time pressure
To eliminate candidates who cannot predict market direction correctly
body.explanation: These rounds are built to compress this course's core reasoning, quoting both sides, managing inventory, and adjusting for the risk that a counterparty is informed, into a live, fast-paced exercise. They are not about predicting direction correctly or reciting memorised material; they specifically reward the kind of adaptable, first-principles reasoning that survives an interviewer changing the setup mid-question.

points: A common hiring funnel runs from a quantitative aptitude test, through a coding round, through one or more live trading game rounds, to technical and behavioural conversations with the desk
Trading game rounds are compressed, live versions of this course's own core material, quoting both sides while pricing in the risk of an informed counterparty
Genuine conceptual understanding, demonstrated by re-deriving an answer when the interviewer changes the numbers, outperforms memorised formulas in these rounds
Campus recruiting from strong quantitative programmes is a major channel in India, with competitive programming and olympiad backgrounds often used as a signal, though not the only path in
Independent projects that replicate this course's own analyses on real NSE data, spread estimation, PIN or VPIN, a backtested quoting simulation, are a concrete way to stand out
The final lesson in this chapter turns from getting hired to what the first few months on a market making desk actually look like once you're in
